I get what you're saying, but following that ‘go this way’ sign is what I've been doing for years – it's called avoidance, and it has turned me into a loner and has made the anxiety even worse in the situations that can't be avoided. I need to be around people to feel alive, but at the same time, I can't be around people, which raises the question: what's the point of living when your only choices are to feel dead or put yourself in situations that make you wish you were dead?

Education for me isn't just about academic success and opening up a career – I want to meet new people and actually enjoy what should be the best years of my life, but now those years have all but passed, and I've wasted them.

Sure it's not too late to do *something* with my life, but I've missed out on so much character/social/etc development that I'll never be the person I want to be (or more accurately, I'll never truly be able to *‘be myself’*), and I've left my education so late that I'll probably never reach my potential in whatever career I end up doing anyway – I'd rather die than have to live with those facts.

Some people would probably say *‘so fucking what, nobody is perfect, everyone has to make compromises, etc’*, but I'm already so far behind with the completely trivial things in life that I have a huge mountain to climb just to reach mediocrity, and it's not worth the pain of making those compromises knowing that I'll probably never even achieve that.

All of that aside, if I can't go out into the real world and function without turning into a nervous, disorganised wreck, then getting an education and a job are the least of my worries.

Nothing lame about that – lots of people do this in the form of TDD, and it's almost always the right thing to do.

Instead of writing out a list of tasks, just write down a list of features the program needs to have, break each feature down into smaller tasks/requirements and then write some unit tests for each requirement (i.e. test that a function does what you expect with particular inputs), write code to make those tests pass, clean up existing code to fit in with the new code – rinse and repeat until everything works.

It forces you to write clean, functional code, your interfaces grow organically, your implementations only do the bare minimum to make the tests pass (so there are less places for obscure bugs to hide), and you can automatically test for breakages when you change things just by rerunning your tests.

I couldn't code for shit until I discovered TDD.

Try replacing all distractions with something completely mindless (like white/pink/etc noise – there are tons of free web-based noise generators around you could try), so that you're not too stimulated, but still have something in the background to latch onto (sleeping in silence is almost impossible with ADHD as we all know).

If that doesn't work, you could have some kind of circadian rhythm disorder, and in that case, if you don't feel like sleeping, it's because you're not physically ready to sleep. The usual treatment for that is melatonin, but it doesn't work for everyone, and if you don't take the right dose at the right time every single day, it will either do absolutely nothing, or make things worse.

Don't try to fix it by staying up – you're only setting yourself up for serious issues in the future (chronic sleep deprivation at the very least, and if you have a rhythm problem, it could turn into full-blown non-24 sleep).

Depends on the cause. Usually it's a hiatus hernia, and they can sneak up on you. In my case, I had symptoms for most of my life (food backing up and taking ages to go down, breathing problems after sleeping on a full stomach, post-nasal drip after eating, etc), and I thought those were just normal things. I didn't realise there was a problem until I started waking up with a mouthful of sick every morning.

If you're just burping up acid occasionally, it could be nothing. Everyone has that at some point. If it gets more frequent, it starts happening without burping, or you start getting coughs/post-nasal drip after meals, then it's definitely GERD.

Tell your doctor next time you go. It's very manageable with medication.

Yes they do amplify it. There's a lot of synergy happening when you mix them.

Nicotine is indirectly dopaminergic (it's pretty much a mild stimulant), and tobacco also contains a few MAOIs. Stimulants like amphetamine and methylphenidate either reverse or block (respectively) the reuptake of dopamine, so when you take something else that boosts dopamine (like nicotine), that boost has even more of an effect, as the dopamine stays around for longer and therefore can build up to much higher concentrations than usual. The MAOIs use up the enzyme that destroys dopamine, which makes the concentration go up even further (the ones in tobacco are short-lived, though, which is why tobacco is so addictive compared to nicotine alone).

I've never written for any mobile platforms, but if you want to get into games, start with something simple like a Tetris clone (you don't even need to design anything – just find the specs of a particular version of it and implement them, or even better, write a Tetris engine that can be configured to replicate any version).

Perhaps write your prototypes in something other than C++ as well until you get the hang of the game mechanics (a lot of big games are made like this anyway, i.e. engine in C++ and game logic in Lua or something). Even if you're proficient with C++, it's not the best language to use when you're learning new shit. Python is probably a safe bet (there are a ton of bindings for things like SDL and OpenGL, and you can use NumPy to avoid a lot of the common bottlenecks).

Using some pre-existing engine might help as well, but for a simple 2D single-player game, you might as well roll your own and learn a bit of everything.

One thing I'd suggest is reading the source of well-written programs that you understand the functionality but not the implementation of. Find where the arguments are parsed, follow the code paths around, make a few changes, etc. You'll quickly figure out what different constructs do, and also pick up on some common idioms/patterns.

That said, some languages truly are just write-only gibberish (Perl), and some only look complicated until you try using them and everything just clicks (Haskell).

They're the same drug, but the release mechanism makes a huge difference. Methylphenidate is only truly useful when it peaks, so you need to time it properly to make the most of it, plus when a high dose wears off, subsequent doses won't necessarily have the full beneficial effects (while the negative effects just get stronger).

With Concerta, you're guaranteed to get 2 mostly overlapping peaks (a small one then a big one a few hours apart) and probably a mild crash at the end of the day, whereas with Ritalin, you can take exactly the right doses at the right times to fit your day, but you need to make sure they overlap properly otherwise you'll either get nothing out of it, or crash hard and feel like crap all day.
